findings.title: Unguarded destructure of window.__workbenchTemplateGating crashes IIFE silently on load-order failure
findings.why_it_matters: The destructure is at module parse/evaluation time inside the IIFE. If workbench-template-gating.js fails to load (network error, CDN miss, wrong script order), window.__workbenchTemplateGating is undefined and the destructure throws a TypeError that silently aborts the entire IIFE — the whole workbench goes dark with no error surfaced to the user or error boundary. The failure mode is invisible because it happens inside a synchronous top-level IIFE evaluation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a guard before the destructure: `if (!window.__workbenchTemplateGating) throw new Error('workbench-template-gating.js must be loaded before workbench.js');` — this converts a silent crash into a legible console error. Longer term, migrate to ES modules to eliminate the load-order dependency entirely.
evidence: web/workbench.js:6996 — `const { BUNDLE_ACTION_ORDER, ... } = window.__workbenchTemplateGating;` — no null check
web/workbench.html:538-539 — script order is the only enforcement mechanism; no integrity check, no defer/async coordination

findings.title: window global used as a cross-file module bus creates implicit load-order contract with no enforcement
findings.why_it_matters: The coupling between workbench-template-gating.js and workbench.js is enforced only by HTML script-tag order. There is no import statement, no bundler dependency graph, and no runtime assertion. Any developer who inserts a new script tag between the two, changes the HTML, or serves workbench.js standalone will reproduce the silent crash. The double-underscore prefix conventionally signals 'private internal', misleading readers about the fact that this is actually a defined cross-file public API surface.
findings.suggested_fix: Migrate to ES modules (type=module / import/export) so the dependency is expressed in the language rather than in HTML. If ES modules are not viable in this deployment context, document the load-order contract explicitly in workbench.html with a comment adjacent to the script tags, and rename the global from __workbenchTemplateGating to a name without the private-convention double underscore (e.g. window.WorkbenchTemplateGating).
evidence: web/workbench.html:538 — `<script src="/workbench-template-gating.js">` placed immediately before workbench.js with no comment explaining the dependency
web/workbench-template-gating.js:98 — `window.__workbenchTemplateGating = { ... }` — double-underscore implies internal/private by JS convention

findings.title: toEqual and toStrictEqual have identical implementations — distinction is unenforceable and misleading
findings.why_it_matters: Both toEqual (line 57) and toStrictEqual (line 64) stringify with JSON.stringify and compare strings. In a real test framework, toStrictEqual additionally checks object type identity (plain object vs class instance), undefined properties, and sparse arrays — the difference matters when testing registry objects. Because the implementations are identical, tests that use toStrictEqual provide no stronger guarantee than toEqual. Future developers adding tests for registry objects that include class instances or undefined-valued keys will write tests that appear strict but are not, producing false confidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Either: (a) remove toStrictEqual and redirect all call sites to toEqual (the honest fix — they do the same thing), or (b) implement toStrictEqual to recursively compare with type and property-descriptor awareness. Option (a) is correct unless the test suite actually needs prototype/class-instance distinctions, which the current fixtures do not.
evidence: tests/web/workbench-template-gating.test.js:57-63 — toEqual body: `const a = JSON.stringify(value); const b = JSON.stringify(expected); if (a !== b) throw`
tests/web/workbench-template-gating.test.js:64-70 — toStrictEqual body: identical to toEqual body

findings.title: Three-environment coordination pattern (browser global / CommonJS require / HTML script order) is an architectural dead end
findings.why_it_matters: The dual-export block at the bottom of workbench-template-gating.js bridges browser and Node.js environments via an if/else on `typeof module`. This works today because workbench-template-gating.js contains only pure functions with no DOM or browser API calls. But the pattern will break the moment any browser-specific symbol (e.g. window, document, CustomEvent) is imported into the file — the Node.js path will throw. The pattern also cannot be linted as a module, cannot be tree-shaken, and cannot be imported by other browser modules. Every new module that needs unit testing will require the same ad hoc dual-export boilerplate.
findings.suggested_fix: Migrate workbench-template-gating.js to an ES module (add `export` keywords, load with `type=module` in HTML, import in tests via a Jest/Node ESM transform or a build step). The dual-export block can then be deleted. This is a larger architectural decision; the current pattern is a known interim compromise and should be documented as such in the file header so future developers do not replicate it.
evidence: web/workbench-template-gating.js:93-99 — dual-export block using typeof module check
tests/web/workbench-template-gating.test.js:17 — `require('../../web/workbench-template-gating')` — CommonJS require of a browser file

residual_risks: The wrapper functions isTemplateActionAuthorable and getEnabledActions in workbench.js close over state.templateRegistry and state.templateSetKey at call time, not at destructure time. This is correct, but the state closure is invisible to callers of the public API — if state.templateRegistry is null (before the template fetch completes), getEnabledActions silently returns {} with no warning. This is a pre-existing state-timing issue not introduced by this PR but now exposed at a seam.

The HTML script-tag ordering is the only enforcement of the load contract. If workbench.html is served through a templating layer (Flask/Jinja) that reorders, bundles, or conditions script tags, the constraint will be broken without any test catching it. There is no integration test that exercises the browser load path.

workbench-template-gating.js has no versioning or API contract mechanism. If isTemplateActionAuthorable gains a new required parameter, workbench.js callers (which forward a fixed set of arguments) will silently pass undefined for the new parameter with no TypeError.
testing_gaps: No test exercises the browser load path — the tests only exercise the CommonJS require path. A script-order regression in workbench.html would not be caught by any test.

No test exercises the wrapper functions in workbench.js (isTemplateActionAuthorable and getEnabledActions). Only the pure implementations in workbench-template-gating.js are tested. The state-injection wiring (passing state.templateRegistry, state.templateSetKey) is untested.
No test covers the behavior when window.__workbenchTemplateGating is undefined at destructure time — the silent crash scenario has no regression coverage.

getEnabledActions ordering guarantee (canonical keys first, remainder after) is tested with at most two keys in the non-canonical position test; there is no test with multiple non-canonical keys to verify stable relative ordering of the remainder.
